item.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Regression for Battery Capacity: Pooling across Cells and Chemistries
item.dc:creator: Anthony Faustine
item.description:
Series: Bayesian Modelling for Industrial Applications, Part 3. Part 1 introduced Bayesian thinking, and Part 2 fitted one Beta regression to the six cells of one chemistry.

An operator of a battery fleet has to decide at every inspection whether to retire a cell or to leave it in service. A cell that has fallen below 80% of its nominal capacity is at the end of its useful life. The operator does not see the state of health directly, only diagnostics measured in the cycle, and a manufacturer that introduces a new chemistry has tested only a few cells of it. Part 2 gave the six cells of one chemistry the same degradation curve. That was a sensible first model, and its test showed the limit: predicted from the other five, four cells were followed closely and two were missed. Cells differ, and cells of one chemistry resemble each other more than they resemble cells of another, so the question is how far a new cell should be believed to resemble the cells that have been seen.

This post answers it with a hierarchical model, in which each cell draws its parameters from its chemistry and each chemistry from the whole fleet. The model is built with PyMC1 and fitted to the CALCE cycling data of Part 2, now with both chemistries. The post shows the priors before and after the data, checks how far the conclusions depend on the prior of the precision, and scores the model against its two obvious alternatives, one curve for all cells and one curve per cell, on the cells that it was fitted to. The hierarchy separates the two chemistries sharply. The second post of Part 3 tests it on two cells that it never saw and turns its predictions into the retirement decision of the operator.

Show the setup of the notebook 
from importlib.metadata import version
import os
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "2")

import arviz as az
import numpy as np
import pymc as pm
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

from bayes import priors
from bayes.data import calce
from bayes.plot import concepts, hierarchy, tables
from bayes.plot.inline import show
from bayes.regression import hierarchical as hier

FAST = os.environ.get("HIER_FAST") == "1"  # a smoke test with a few draws, to check that the notebook runs
CACHE = Path("cache-fast" if FAST else "cache")
CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
FEATURES = ["charge_current_auc", "charge_current_mean", "discharge_voltage_auc", "discharge_voltage_crest"]
HELD_OUT = ["CS2_38", "CX2_38"]  # the last cell of each chemistry, kept back for the tests of the next post
MAIN = {"draws": 40 if FAST else 500, "tune": 40 if FAST else 750, "chains": 2 if FAST else 4}
REFIT = {"draws": 40 if FAST else 500, "tune": 40 if FAST else 750, "chains": 2 if FAST else 4}
PHI_PRIORS = {  # log-normal priors of the precision: the mean and standard deviation of its logarithm
    "Narrow": (float(np.log(100.0)), 0.3),  # centred on 100
    "Default": (float(np.log(100.0)), 1.0),  # centred on 100
    "Wide": (float(np.log(1000.0)), 1.5),  # centred on 1,000
}
print("pymc", version("pymc"), "| arviz", version("arviz"), "| fast mode:", FAST)
Show the loading of the data 
data = calce.load(Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "calce-battery-features.parquet", FEATURES, every=8)
train, held_out = calce.split(data, HELD_OUT)
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(train[FEATURES])  # standardised on the training cells only
CHEMISTRIES = list(dict.fromkeys(data["CellType"]))
COLOURS = hierarchy.palette(CHEMISTRIES)
CHEMISTRY_OF = data.drop_duplicates("cell").set_index("cell")["CellType"].to_dict()

summary = data.groupby(["CellType", "cell"]).agg(rows=("cycle", "size"), last_cycle=("cycle", "max"))
for chemistry, rows in summary.groupby("CellType"):
    print(
        f"{chemistry}: {len(rows)} cells, {rows['rows'].min()} to {rows['rows'].max()} kept cycles per cell, longest life {rows['last_cycle'].max()} cycles"
    )
print(
    f"{len(data):,} cycles kept; {len(train):,} in the {train['cell'].nunique()} training cells; held out: {', '.join(HELD_OUT)}"
)
print(f"SoH above 100%: {(data['soh'] > 100).mean():.1%} of the kept cycles")

Levels of Pooling

The question of how far a new cell resembles the cells already seen has three answers, which are called levels of pooling, and Figure 1 draws them for the 13 cells of this study. Under complete pooling every cell shares one set of curve parameters, so a new cell receives the average curve of the fleet and its chemistry plays no part. Under no pooling each cell has parameters of its own and nothing is shared, so a cell is described by its own record only, and a cell without a record is described by the prior. Partial pooling lies between them: the parameters of a cell come from a distribution that belongs to its chemistry, and the parameters of a chemistry come from a distribution over the fleet. A cell with a long record is then free to move away from its chemistry, and a cell with a short or incomplete record is drawn towards it.

Show the code of the figure 
for diagram in (concepts.complete, concepts.none, concepts.partial):
    show(diagram(CHEMISTRY_OF, HELD_OUT, COLOURS))

The three diagrams differ in what lies above the cells and so in what each strategy believes about a cell that it has not seen. The hollow rings are the two cells that are held out of the fits to test that belief, one of each chemistry. Complete pooling has no way to tell the new cells apart, no pooling has nothing to say about them except the prior, and partial pooling starts each of them from the level of its own chemistry. The choice matters most when records are short or incomplete, because the data then say little about a cell and the structure of the model decides what is believed. The sections that follow measure that on a real fleet, and the first of them describes the data.

Thirteen Cells, Two Chemistries

The data are the cycle-by-cycle diagnostics of 13 lithium-ion cells from the CALCE laboratory, in the form prepared for Part 2.2 Six cells are of chemistry CS2, with a nominal capacity of 1.10 Ah, and seven are of chemistry CX2, with 1.35 Ah. Every cell was cycled until it fell well below the end-of-life threshold of 80% state of health (SoH). The target is the SoH, the capacity divided by the nominal capacity, divided again by 1.1 so that it stays inside the open unit interval that a Beta likelihood requires. SoH exceeds 100% in 1.7% of the cycles, which the ceiling of 1.1 accommodates. The inputs are the four diagnostics of Part 2, standardised on the training cells only.

Every eighth cycle is kept, because neighbouring cycles are almost duplicates, which leaves 1,752 observations with between 78 and 196 per cell. Two cells, CS2_38 and CX2_38, the last of each chemistry, are held out to test the strategies on cells that the model has not seen, and the remaining 11 cells provide 1,456 observations for training. The inputs are measured in the same cycle as the capacity, which is what an operator has at an inspection, so the model estimates the state of health from diagnostics and does not forecast it.

Show the code of the figure 
show(lambda: hierarchy.curves(data, HELD_OUT, COLOURS))

The two chemistries differ markedly, as Figure 2 shows. The CX2 cells last up to 2,474 cycles and decline slowly, while the CS2 cells fail between 737 and 1,056 cycles. The records are not equally complete. CX2_16 begins at cycle 463 with a state of health of 94%, and CX2_33 begins at cycle 187, so for these two cells the early part of the curve is not observed. What the data say about their initial level is little, and a model that sees only these cells has to rely on its prior.

The Hierarchical Model

The observation layer is a Beta regression, as in Part 2.3 The state of health yijy_{ij} of cell jj at its cycle cijc_{ij} follows a Beta distribution with mean μij\mu_{ij} and precision ϕ\phi,

yij∼Beta(μijϕ,(1−μij)ϕ), y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Beta}\big(\mu_{ij}\phi,\ (1-\mu_{ij})\phi\big),

and the mean is linked to the linear predictor by the inverse logit,

μij=logit−1(ηij). \mu_{ij} = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\eta_{ij}).

The linear predictor on the logit scale combines the ageing of the cell with the diagnostics 𝒙ij\mathbf{x}_{ij},

ηij=αj−Akgj(cij)+𝒙ij⊤𝜷, \eta_{ij} = \alpha_j - A_k\, g_j(c_{ij}) + \mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta},

where ageing is a saturating exponential of the cycle,

gj(c)=1−e−λjc. g_j(c) = 1 - e^{-\lambda_j c}.

Here αj\alpha_j is the initial level of cell jj, λj\lambda_j its rate, AkA_k the amplitude of the chemistry kk to which it belongs, and the cycle is counted in thousands. The hierarchy ties the cell parameters to the chemistry. Each chemistry has an initial level aka_k, a log rate ℓk\ell_k and an amplitude AkA_k, drawn from distributions that are shared by the fleet, and a cell departs from its chemistry by an offset,

αj=ak+σa,kza,j, \alpha_j = a_k + \sigma_{a,k}\, z_{a,j},

log⁡λj=ℓk+σℓ,kzℓ,j, \log\lambda_j = \ell_k + \sigma_{\ell,k}\, z_{\ell,j},

where the offsets za,jz_{a,j} and zℓ,jz_{\ell,j} have a standard normal distribution.

The unit-normal offsets zz are sampled and scaled afterwards, which is known as a non-centred parameterisation. It matters when the spread between cells is small, because a model that samples αj\alpha_j directly then has a funnel-shaped posterior that the sampler traverses poorly and reports as divergences.4

The code defines one function for the three strategies, so that they differ in nothing else. For complete pooling the three parameters are single numbers, for no pooling each cell has its own with an independent prior, and for partial pooling they follow the hierarchy above. The hidden cell below builds the three models and fits them, as the section on sampling describes.

Show the model and its fits 
models = {
    pooling_level: hier.hierarchical_model(train, scaler, FEATURES, pooling_level) for pooling_level in hier.POOLING
}
print({pooling_level: len(model.free_RVs) for pooling_level, model in models.items()})
fits = {
    pooling_level: hier.sample(
        models[pooling_level], CACHE / f"train-{pooling_level}.nc", seed=2026 + index, log_likelihood=True, **MAIN
    )
    for index, pooling_level in enumerate(hier.POOLING)
}

Priors and Prior Checks

A prior states what the model believes before it sees any data, and the quickest way to understand one is to look at it. Figure 3 draws the prior of each quantity that the model learns. The priors are weakly informative, which means that they rule out values that no battery could show and leave the rest to the data.5 The initial level has a normal prior centred on 2 with a standard deviation of 1 at the fleet level, which puts the state of health near 97% for a cell with no ageing term and no diagnostic effect. The log rate is centred on log⁡5\log 5 per thousand cycles with a standard deviation of 0.5, so the saturating term of an ageing cell reaches half of its amplitude after about 140 cycles. The amplitude has a half-normal prior, which allows a small ageing term or a large one but not a negative one. The effect of each standardised diagnostic has a normal prior with a standard deviation of 0.2, so that a feature has to earn a large coefficient, and the standard deviations between cells and between chemistries have half-normal priors, as is usual for scale parameters. The precision ϕ\phi of the Beta likelihood has a log-normal prior centred on 100, which corresponds to noise of about 5 points of state of health at mid-life. Table 1 lists them all.

Show the code 
display(tables.themed_gt(priors.hierarchical()))
Show the draws of the prior 
with models["partial"]:
    prior = pm.sample_prior_predictive(draws=500, random_seed=1)
    prior_many = pm.sample_prior_predictive(draws=3000, random_seed=2)
prior_soh = prior.prior_predictive["y"].to_numpy().ravel() * hier.CEILING * 100
drawn = np.random.default_rng(1).choice(prior_soh, size=min(20000, prior_soh.size), replace=False)
update = hier.prior_posterior(prior_many, fits["partial"])
QUANTITIES = list(hier.PRIOR_LEVELS.values()) + ["Precision (log10)"]
Show the code of the figure 
for quantity in QUANTITIES:
    show(lambda quantity=quantity: hierarchy.priors(update[update["source"] == "Prior"], quantity, COLOURS))

The four priors are broad on purpose. The initial level and the log rate cover every ageing curve that a lithium-ion cell could plausibly follow, the amplitude allows any size of ageing term, and the precision prior expects the noise of a fair sensor, not of a cell that one diagnostic describes almost exactly. A prior that is broad in this way commits the model to very little, and the posterior shows how much the data then changed it. What the four priors imply together for the state of health can be checked before any data are used, by drawing parameters from the priors and simulating the cells that they describe. Figure 4 compares the state of health of that prior predictive distribution with the observed values of the training cells.

Show the code of the figure 
show(lambda: hierarchy.prior(train["soh"].to_numpy(), drawn))

The prior has its 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles at 23.6%, 91.1% and 109.1%, against 50.8%, 81.9% and 97.7% in the data. It is wider than the data at both ends and its median lies nine points above the observed one, and some of its mass exceeds 100%, which the data also do in 1.7% of the cycles. A weak prior should rule out the impossible and leave the rest to the data, and this one does.

Posterior Sampling

The posteriors are sampled with the No-U-Turn sampler.6 Every fit runs four chains of 500 draws after 750 tuning draws, with a target acceptance rate of 0.90. This post fits the three models of the training cells and two refits for the check of the prior, and the next post refits the models for the test of new cells. Sampling is the slow part, with each hierarchical fit taking several minutes on a laptop, so the notebook stores each fit in a cache folder and reads it back on a repeat run.

Convergence of the Chains

None of the three fits on the training cells has a divergent transition. The worst R̂\hat{R}, the disagreement between chains, is 1.000 for partial pooling, 1.010 for complete pooling and 1.020 for no pooling, against a common guide of 1.01,7 and the smallest bulk effective sample sizes are 820, 1,008 and 392, so the no-pooling model is the least well behaved. The two refits of the check of the prior, which is described below, have a worst R̂\hat{R} of 1.01 and a smallest bulk effective sample size of 769. Two divergent transitions occur in the 4,000 draws of the refit under the wide prior, and its estimates agree with those of the other fits, as the check of the prior shows.

Show the checks of the sampler 
for pooling_level, idata in fits.items():
    report = hier.convergence(idata)
    print(
        f"{pooling_level}: {idata.posterior.sizes['chain']} chains of {idata.posterior.sizes['draw']} draws, {report['divergences']} divergences, max R-hat {report['r_hat']:.3f}, min ESS bulk {report['ess_bulk']:.0f}, min ESS tail {report['ess_tail']:.0f}"
    )

From Prior to Posterior

The data turn each prior into a posterior, and the distance between the two says how much the data taught the model. Figure 5 draws the log rate of each chemistry and the precision, each against its prior. Where a posterior is narrow and far from the prior, the data decided the answer, and where it stays close to the prior, the prior did. The first quantity decides how quickly the ageing term of a chemistry saturates, and the second decides how closely the model believes that its predictions follow the observations, so together they show where the data were informative and where they were not.

Show the code of the figure 
for quantity in ("Log rate (per 1,000 cycles)", "Precision (log10)"):
    show(lambda quantity=quantity: hierarchy.priors(update, quantity, COLOURS))

The log rate of the two chemistries moved well away from the prior, which is centred on log⁡5=1.61\log 5 = 1.61. The posterior mean is −0.31-0.31 for CS2 and 0.73 for CX2, so the data separated the chemistries and placed both well below the prior. The posterior of CS2 is the broader of the two, with a 90% interval from −0.78-0.78 to 0.30 against 0.44 to 1.05 for CX2, because fewer cells inform it and they differ from one another. The precision moved furthest. Its posterior mean is 1,810 against a prior centred on 100, and the prior puts only 0.2% of its mass above that value, so the figure shows it on a logarithmic scale, where the posterior is a narrow spike at 3.26 far to the right of a prior centred on 2. The data are therefore far more precise than the prior expected, because one diagnostic nearly determines the state of health. This is the one prior of the model that the data contradict, and a later section tests whether it matters.

Posterior of the Chemistries

The chemistry level of the hierarchical model is where the model says something that a single curve cannot. Figure 6 shows the posterior of the three parameters for each chemistry, one parameter in each panel. They differ in all three. The initial level is 1.19 for CS2 (90% interval 1.08 to 1.32) and 1.98 for CX2 (1.72 to 2.22) on the logit scale. The amplitude of the saturating term is 2.76 for CS2 (2.33 to 3.29) and 1.03 for CX2 (1.01 to 1.06). The log rate is −0.31-0.31 for CS2 (from −0.78-0.78 to 0.30) and 0.73 for CX2 (from 0.44 to 1.05), and the posterior probability that the rate of CX2 exceeds that of CS2 is 0.992.

Show the code of the figure 
draws = hier.chemistry_draws(fits["partial"])
for quantity in hier.PRIOR_LEVELS.values():
    show(lambda quantity=quantity: hierarchy.chemistry(draws, COLOURS, quantity))

Read together, the three describe the curves of Figure 2. The CX2 term is small and saturates early, with a half-time of about 330 cycles, so the long, slow decline of those cells is carried by the diagnostics. The CS2 term is large and slow, with a half-time of about 950 cycles, so those cells keep losing capacity over their whole life. The difference between the chemistries is larger than the difference between cells within one. The standard deviation between cells of the log rate is 0.52 in CS2 and 0.47 in CX2, against a gap of 1.04 between the chemistries, and for the initial level it is 0.14 and 0.34, against a gap of 0.79. Only two chemistries inform these standard deviations, so they are set partly by their priors and are not interpreted further.

Of the four diagnostics, only the area under the discharge voltage has an effect that differs from zero beyond doubt, at 0.362 with a posterior standard deviation of 0.016, and the other three lie within two standard deviations of zero. The precision ϕ\phi is about 1,800, which corresponds to a noise standard deviation of about one point of state of health. That is far in the upper tail of its prior, which puts 0.2% of its mass above 1,800, and it says that one diagnostic nearly determines the state of health, which has consequences for the tests that follow.

Cell Shrinkage

The hierarchy also changes what is said about a single cell. Figure 7 sets the estimate of each training cell without pooling, hollow, beside the estimate with partial pooling, filled, with the posterior mean of the chemistry as a dashed line.

Show the code of the figure 
chemistry_of = train.drop_duplicates("cell").set_index("cell")["CellType"]
cells = [cell for chemistry in CHEMISTRIES for cell in chemistry_of[chemistry_of == chemistry].index]
estimates, means = hier.shrinkage_frames(fits["none"], fits["partial"], chemistry_of, cells)
for parameter in ("Initial level (logit)", "Log rate (per 1,000 cycles)"):
    show(lambda parameter=parameter: hierarchy.shrinkage(estimates, means, COLOURS, cells, parameter))

The largest change is for the cell with the least complete record. The initial level of CX2_16, whose record begins at cycle 463, moves from 3.54 without pooling to 1.96 with it, close to the 1.98 of its chemistry, and CX2_33, which begins at cycle 187, moves from 2.09 to 1.74. The other cells change by 0.12 or less. Without pooling, the initial level of a cell with no early record is set by the prior and by observations far from cycle zero, and the hierarchy replaces that with what its chemistry shows.

The log rate changes more widely, by up to 0.94 in CS2_35 and 0.92 in CS2_33, although those cells have complete records. On a curve that has not yet saturated, the rate and the amplitude trade off against each other, so a cell’s rate is poorly determined on its own, and the shared amplitude of its chemistry fixes part of that trade. This reading is consistent with the figure but was not tested separately. Averaged over the training cells, an estimate differs by 0.24 logit units for the initial level and by 0.40 for the log rate between the two strategies.

Sensitivity to the Prior

The posterior of the precision lies far from its prior, and a prior that is far from the data can decide the answer when the data are few. With 1,456 observations that is unlikely, but the question can be answered by computation and the limits of the first version of this study left it open. The model is therefore refitted with a narrow prior for the precision, a log-normal distribution centred on 100 whose logarithm has a standard deviation of 0.3, and with a wide prior centred on 1,000 whose logarithm has a standard deviation of 1.5, against the default of 1.0 centred on 100. Figure 8 draws the posterior of the log rate of each chemistry under the three priors, with the default fit as the heavier line.

Show the refits under other priors 
sensitivity_fits = {}
for index, (setting, phi_prior) in enumerate(PHI_PRIORS.items()):
    if setting.startswith("Default"):
        sensitivity_fits[setting] = fits["partial"]  # the fit of the post, not a second copy of it
        continue
    model = hier.hierarchical_model(train, scaler, FEATURES, "partial", phi_prior=phi_prior)
    sensitivity_fits[setting] = hier.sample(
        model, CACHE / f"prior-phi-{setting.split(',')[0].lower()}.nc", seed=4000 + index, **REFIT
    )
sensitivity = hier.prior_sensitivity(sensitivity_fits)
sensitivity_draws = hier.sensitivity_draws(sensitivity_fits)
for setting, idata in sensitivity_fits.items():
    report = hier.convergence(idata)
    print(
        f"{setting}: {report['divergences']} divergences, max R-hat {report['r_hat']:.3f}, min ESS bulk {report['ess_bulk']:.0f}"
    )
Show the code of the figure 
for chemistry in CHEMISTRIES:
    show(lambda chemistry=chemistry: hierarchy.sensitivity(sensitivity_draws, chemistry))

The three curves of each chemistry lie almost on top of one another. The posterior mean of the log rate of CS2 is −0.36-0.36, −0.32-0.32 and −0.33-0.33 under the narrow, the default and the wide prior, and that of CX2 is 0.73, 0.73 and 0.74. The probability that the rate of CX2 exceeds that of CS2 is 0.996, 0.992 and 0.990. The initial level and the amplitude of each chemistry agree to within 0.02 across the three priors. The posterior mean of the precision is 1,739, 1,810 and 1,820, which says that the data move the precision from a prior centred on 100 to about 1,800 even when the prior is tight. The conclusions about the chemistries therefore do not depend on the prior of the precision, and the tight prior of the default model does not decide them. The same parameter sets the width of every predictive interval, which the next post checks on the scores.

Fit on Training Cells

Before the model is tested on cells that it has not seen, it is checked on the cells that it has. Leave-one-out cross-validation scores a model by the log density that it gives to an observation when that observation is left out of the fit, and the average of these scores is the expected log predictive density.8 Pareto-smoothed importance sampling approximates the scores from a single fit, and the difference between two models comes with a standard error. The log density is a proper scoring rule, so the model with the larger value is the one whose predictive distribution lies closer to the process that generated the data. Its scale is that of the Beta density of the state of health as a fraction, so only differences between models have a meaning. Figure 9 shows, for each of the 11 training cells, how much partial pooling and complete pooling gain over no pooling, and the bars of one model add up to its difference in expected log predictive density. Partial pooling is behind no pooling by 124.6 (standard error 14.5), which is 8.6 standard errors, and complete pooling is behind by 2,242 (standard error 76). Partial pooling is behind in 10 of the 11 cells and its largest loss is 31.3 for CX2_16, while complete pooling is behind in every cell. The effective number of parameters is 63.6 for no pooling, 45.9 for partial pooling and 10.5 for complete pooling. One observation of the no-pooling model and one of the partial-pooling model have a Pareto kk above 0.7, so those two totals are a little less certain than the standard errors say.

Show the leave-one-out scores 
labels = {"none": "No pooling", "complete": "Complete pooling", "partial": "Partial pooling"}
named = {labels[pooling_level]: fits[pooling_level] for pooling_level in hier.POOLING}
comparison = az.compare(named, ic="loo")
print(comparison[["elpd_loo", "p_loo", "elpd_diff", "dse"]].round(1).to_string())
by_cell = hier.loo_by_cell(named, train["cell"].to_numpy())
wide = by_cell.pivot(index="cell", columns="method", values="elpd")
gain = wide.sub(wide["No pooling"], axis=0)
print("cells where partial pooling beats no pooling:", int((gain["Partial pooling"] > 0).sum()), "of", len(gain))
print("largest loss of partial pooling:", gain["Partial pooling"].idxmin(), round(gain["Partial pooling"].min(), 1))
print("cells where complete pooling beats no pooling:", int((gain["Complete pooling"] > 0).sum()))
print("observations with Pareto k above 0.7:", by_cell.groupby("method")["bad"].sum().to_dict())
Show the code of the figure 
for method in ("Partial pooling", "Complete pooling"):
    show(lambda method=method: hierarchy.loo(by_cell, COLOURS, CHEMISTRY_OF, method, "No pooling"))

Cell-specific parameters matter a great deal for cells that are in the data, and the likelihood is so sharp that an offset of two or three points of state of health is worth many units of log density, which is why every cell loses under complete pooling. The same parameters are not available for a new cell, so this ranking does not carry over to one. Leave-one-out here leaves out single cycles, and the neighbouring cycles of the same cell still fix its curve, so it measures how well a model interpolates within cells it has seen and not how well it predicts a cell that it has not. The test of the next post leaves out whole cells and answers that question; a leave-one-cell-out version of this figure would need one refit for each of the 11 cells and each model.

Limits of the Study

The prior of the precision ϕ\phi is tight and the posterior lies far in its upper tail, and the refits above show that the conclusions about the chemistries do not depend on it. Two chemistries are few, because the spread between chemistries is estimated from two groups, so the chemistry-level standard deviations are set partly by their priors and are not interpreted here. The curve is simple, since a saturating exponential with a linear effect of the diagnostics has no knee, which the end of life of these cells shows, and every eighth cycle is used, which shortens the run and discards little, although the observations that remain are still correlated. The residuals are treated as independent, and the next post shows what that costs when the model predicts a cell that it has not seen. The leave-one-out scores of the last section leave out single cycles, so they measure interpolation within the cells of the data and not prediction of a new cell.

Summary of Findings

A hierarchical model with cells in chemistries separates what belongs to a chemistry from what belongs to a cell. The two chemistries differ in all three curve parameters, with a probability of 0.992 that CX2 has the higher rate, and the conclusion does not change under a narrower or a wider prior for the precision. Partial pooling also steadies the cell whose early life is missing, CX2_16, whose initial level falls from 3.54 to 1.96.

The fit to the cells that the model has seen favours cell-specific parameters, as it should. In leave-one-out cross-validation partial pooling is behind no pooling in 10 of the 11 cells, because the cells in the data fix their own curves, and complete pooling is behind in every cell. That ranking says how well a model interpolates within cells that it has seen and not how it predicts a new one. The second post of Part 3 leaves out whole cells, tests the three strategies as predictors of a new cell, and applies the cost-loss rule of an operator to their probabilities.

Reproducible Results

The notebook is in the bayesian-modelling repository and runs from the first cell to the last in the uv environment of the repository, with PyMC 5.25, ArviZ 0.22 and lets-plot 4.11, and downloads the feature file when it first runs. The model, the sampling and the figures are functions of the bayes package, which has unit tests, and the cells of the notebook only call them. The sampling settings are in the first cell, and setting the environment variable HIER_FAST=1 runs the whole notebook with a few draws in a minute or two, to check that it works before the full run. The fits are stored in cache/, so a repeat of the full run reads them back.

Show the numbers quoted in the text 
# Numbers that the text quotes. This cell prints them and is hidden on the page.
posterior = fits["partial"].posterior
print(
    f"Prior predictive SoH percentiles 5/50/95: {np.percentile(prior_soh, [5, 50, 95]).round(1)}; observed {np.percentile(train['soh'], [5, 50, 95]).round(1)}"
)
for quantity, draws in (
    ("log rate", posterior["loglambda_chem"]),

    first, second = (draws.sel(chemistry=name).to_numpy().ravel() for name in CHEMISTRIES)
    print(
        f"{quantity}: {CHEMISTRIES[0]} {first.mean():.2f} ({np.percentile(first, 5):.2f} to {np.percentile(first, 95):.2f}), {CHEMISTRIES[1]} {second.mean():.2f} ({np.percentile(second, 5):.2f} to {np.percentile(second, 95):.2f}), P({CHEMISTRIES[1]} > {CHEMISTRIES[0]}) = {(second > first).mean():.3f}"
    )
print(

            round(float(posterior["beta"].sel(feature=name).mean()), 3),

    round(float(posterior["phi"].mean()), 1),
    "| sigma_cell_alpha",
    posterior["sigma_cell_alpha"].mean(("chain", "draw")).to_numpy().round(2),
    "| sigma_cell_lambda",
    posterior["sigma_cell_lambda"].mean(("chain", "draw")).to_numpy().round(2),

print(
    "prior P(phi > posterior mean):",
    round(
        float(
            (

control = az.from_netcdf(CACHE / "train-control.nc")
print("control (complete pooling, no diagnostics): phi mean", round(float(control.posterior["phi"].mean()), 1))

    .mean()
    .round(2)
    .to_dict(),

print("sensitivity:")
print(sensitivity.round(3).to_string(index=False))
for setting, idata in sensitivity_fits.items():
    p = idata.posterior["loglambda_chem"].stack(s=("chain", "draw"))

        setting,

        round(float((p.sel(chemistry=CHEMISTRIES[1]) > p.sel(chemistry=CHEMISTRIES[0])).mean()), 3),

item.title: Choosing the Lookback Window, Lags and Inputs of a Forecaster
item.dc:creator: Anthony Faustine
item.description:
Inputs of a Forecaster

Before a model predicts tomorrow’s load, someone has to decide what it may look at: how many recent observations to give it as a window, which older values to add beside them, and which other inputs, such as the hour, the weekday or the temperature, to include. These choices usually come from habit, a week of history because a week feels natural, or from trial and error on the test set, which lets the test period shape a model that is meant to be judged on it.

This post makes all three choices from the training data alone, using functions of the open-source library twiga.[1] The autocorrelation sets the window and proposes the lags. The lags, the calendar variables and the weather inputs are then ranked by six measures of relevance, first within each group and then together. A column of random noise sits among the candidates as a control, because a ranking that places noise high cannot be trusted. Four series with different character serve as examples: the half-hourly demand of one London household, the hourly charging of electric vehicles (EV) across Los Angeles, the output of a photovoltaic (PV) array, and the net load of the site that the array feeds.

No forecaster is trained, so the post makes no claim about accuracy. Its claim is narrower: the choices can be made without touching the test period, every step can be inspected, and the result behaves sensibly on a control. The code is folded under each figure, and every selection function is imported from twiga 1.1.8 and not rewritten.

Show the code

Lookback Window and Lags

A forecaster that predicts the next day from what is known at the forecast origin draws on the history of its target in two ways. The lookback window is a block of the WW most recent observations, ending at the origin. A lag of kk steps adds the value yt−ky_{t-k}, which reaches further back than the window without making it longer. A lag can be used only if its value exists at the origin, so every lag is at least one step. Figure 2 shows a window, the horizon and three lags for a forecast one day ahead.

Each choice has a price. A window that is too short hides the daily shape, while a window that is too long, or a lag that repeats what the window already holds, hands the model the same information twice and raises its variance without adding signal. The autocorrelation function (ACF) gives a principled starting point.[5] It is the correlation of the series with itself kk steps earlier,

ρk=Cov⁡(yt,yt−k)Var⁡(yt), \rho_k = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(y_t,\, y_{t-k})}{\operatorname{Var}(y_t)},

and its peaks fall at the periods in which the series repeats. The shortest significant peak sets the window, because it is the shortest span over which the dynamics repeat, and the longer peaks become lag candidates. A lag as long as the shortest period would only repeat the window, so it is left out. A value of ρk\rho_k counts as significant when it lies outside the band ±1.96/T\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}, the range expected for a series of length TT with no autocorrelation.

Six Measures of Relevance

An input is relevant to the extent that it tells something about the target, and no single measure sees every kind of dependence. twiga therefore scores each candidate in six ways:

  • the absolute Spearman rank correlation, which detects any monotone relation;
  • the F statistic of a linear fit, which detects a linear relation;
  • the mutual information, which detects any relation visible in the joint histogram of the two variables;
  • Chatterjee’s ξ\xi, a rank-based coefficient that is zero under independence and one when one variable is a function of the other, whatever its shape;[6]
  • the predictive power score, the gain of a small decision tree fitted on the candidate alone over predicting the mean of the target;
  • the impurity importance of a random forest, which also picks up interactions between inputs.[7]

Consider a load that rises when the temperature departs from a comfortable value in either direction. The rank correlation and the F statistic cannot see that relation and the other four can, so a ranking built on one measure inherits the blind spot of that measure.

The six scores lie on different scales, so each is converted into a ranking and the rankings are combined, which is known as rank aggregation.[8] Under the Borda count a measure gives the best of mm candidates mm points, the next best m−1m-1 points, and so on, and the score of a candidate is its total over the measures. Writing rijr_{ij} for the points that measure jj gives candidate ii,

Bi=∑jrij. B_i = \sum_{j} r_{ij}.

A sum like this counts measures that repeat each other twice. The rank correlation and the F statistic, for instance, usually order candidates alike. twiga therefore also offers a weighted sum, Si=∑jwjrijS_i = \sum_j w_j\, r_{ij}, in which the weight wjw_j is proportional to 1−ρ‾j1 - \bar{\rho}_j, where ρ‾j\bar{\rho}_j is the mean absolute Spearman correlation between the scores of measure jj and those of the other five. The weights have a floor of 0.05 and sum to one. The default of the library is the equal-weight sum, and the figures below use the weighted one, the option weighted_borda.

Two more choices complete the set-up. Each cyclic calendar variable enters as a sine and a cosine, so that 23:00 lies next to 00:00,[9] and a column of standard normal noise joins the candidates, since any measure that ranks it above a real input overstates relevance.

Figure 5 shows how far the six measures agree on the net load. Mutual information and ξ\xi agree most, at 0.98, and the predictive power and the forest importance least, at 0.65, so the weights stay between 0.14 and 0.19 here and between 0.13 and 0.25 across the four series, the largest being that of the forest importance on the PV output. Because the measures overlap only in part, the weights differ little from equal ones, and a later section measures how little.

Ranking within Subgroups

The candidates fall into three kinds that answer different questions: the lags and rolling means of the target, the calendar variables, and the known inputs such as the weather. It is natural to rank each kind on its own first, because the question within a kind is which one is best, which lag or which calendar encoding. This is also how twiga’s dataset loader selects inputs. Each subgroup is ranked by the six measures with the equal-weight Borda count, and the noise column joins every subgroup as a control.

Figure 6 shows the three rankings for the net load. Each tile gives the position that one measure assigns, with 1 the best and the darkest blue, and the last column is the Borda total, in which a higher number is better.

Show the code 
def short(feature: str) -> str:
    """Compact row label for the subgroup panels: 2-day lag, 7-day mean, and the calendar and input labels."""
    days = lambda steps: int(steps) // SERIES["Net load"]["samples"]  # noqa: E731
    if "_lag_" in feature:
        return f"{days(feature.rsplit('_', 1)[1])}-day lag"
    if "_rolling_mean_win_" in feature:
        return f"{days(feature.rsplit('_', 1)[1])}-day mean"
    return FIELDS.get(feature, feature)


def group_panel(frame: pd.DataFrame, group: str, features: list[str], target: str, tag: str, height: int):
    """Rank within one subgroup, with the noise column as its control: a heat panel of the rank under each measure."""
    scores, _ = rank(frame, features + ["noise"], target, aggregation="borda_count")
    ranks = scores[RANKERS].fillna(0).rank(ascending=False, method="first").astype(int)
    order = scores["borda_count"].sort_values(ascending=False).index.tolist()
    m = len(order)
    rows = [
        (short(f), {"abs_corr": "Corr", "f_score": "F", "mi_score": "MI", "xi_score": "Xi", "pps_score": "PPS", "rf_importance": "RF"}[r], int(ranks.loc[f, r]), 1 - (ranks.loc[f, r] - 1) / (m - 1))
        for f in order for r in RANKERS
    ]
    cells = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["row", "column", "rank", "shade"])
    cells["ink"] = np.where(cells["shade"] > 0.55, "white", INK)
    columns = list(dict.fromkeys(cells["column"]))
    fused = pd.DataFrame({"row": [short(f) for f in order], "column": "Sum", "label": [f"{scores.loc[f, 'borda_count']:.0f}" for f in order]})
    names = [short(f) for f in order]
    pad = ["\u200b" * (i + 1) for i in range(height - m)]
    control = cells[cells["row"] == short("noise")]
    sums = fused.assign(shade=0.0)
    plot = (
        ggplot(cells, aes("column", "row"))
        + geom_tile(aes(fill="shade"), color="white", size=1.0)
        + scale_fill_gradient(low=tint(BLUE, 0.94), high=BLUE, limits=[0, 1])
        + geom_tile(data=sums, mapping=aes("column", "row"), fill=tint(SLATE, 0.88), color="white", size=1.0, inherit_aes=False)
        + geom_tile(data=control, mapping=aes("column", "row"), fill="rgba(0,0,0,0)", color=ORANGE, size=1.1, inherit_aes=False)
        + geom_text(aes(label="rank", color="ink"), size=5.4, family=FONT)
        + scale_color_manual(values={"white": "white", INK: INK})
        + geom_text(aes("column", "row", label="label"), data=fused, size=5.4, family=FONT, color=INK, fontface="bold", inherit_aes=False)
        + scale_x_discrete(limits=columns + ["Sum"], position="top", expand=[0.0, 0.8])
        + scale_y_discrete(limits=pad + names[::-1])
        + labs(title=f"({tag}) {group}", x="", y="")
        + house()
        + theme(axis_line=element_blank(), axis_ticks=element_blank(), plot_title=element_text(face="bold", size=12, hjust=0), axis_text_x=element_text(size=9.5, angle=0))
    )
    return plot, scores

for tag, (group, features) in zip("abc", groups.items()):

For the net load, the lag of two days heads the lags and means, ahead of the lags of seven and three days and the two means, with noise last. Among the calendar variables the sine of the hour is first, the cosine of the day of the year second and the cosine of the hour third. Both weekday encodings fall below the day of the year, and noise is last again. Among the known inputs the solar radiation comes first and the air temperature second, both ahead of the noise.

The three rankings could be used as they stand, with a fixed quota from each subgroup: the best two lags or means, the best two calendar variables and the best known input. Set against the single ranking of all candidates, which the next section builds, that rule selects the same inputs for the household and the EV charging, where it picks four, and shares three of five for the PV output and the net load. In those two series the quota keeps two calendar variables that rank seventh to ninth of fourteen once everything competes. It drops the lag of three days for the net load, which ranks third, and the panel temperature for the PV array, which ranks fourth. Every input it keeps still ranks above the noise column.

Show the code 
def per_group_rule(name: str) -> list[str]:
    """The best two lags or means, the best two calendar inputs and the best known input, each ranked within its subgroup."""
    frame, groups, target = design(name)
    picks = []
    for group, features in groups.items():
        if not features:
            continue
        scores, _ = rank(frame, features + ["noise"], target, aggregation="borda_count")
        ordered = [f for f in scores["borda_count"].sort_values(ascending=False).index if f != "noise"]
        picks += ordered[: 1 if group == "Known inputs" else 2]
    return picks


for name, (scores, _) in results.items():
    pooled_order = scores["weighted_borda"].sort_values(ascending=False).index.tolist()
    picks = per_group_rule(name)
    position = {f: pooled_order.index(f) + 1 for f in picks}
    below_noise = [label(f, name) for f in picks if position[f] > pooled_order.index("noise") + 1]
    print(f"{name}: per-subgroup picks {[label(f, name) for f in picks]}; positions in the pooled order {list(position.values())}; shared with the pooled top {len(picks)}: {len(set(picks) & set(pooled_order[: len(picks)]))}; below the noise column: {below_noise or 'none'}")

Pooled Ranking

Ranking everything together lets a lag compete with a calendar variable and a weather column on one scale. The ranking reads the first 70% of each series and uses the diversity-weighted sum. It covers twelve candidates for the household and the charging, and fourteen for the PV output and the net load.

Figure 7 draws the score of every candidate, best at the top, with the five best in blue and the noise column in orange. Five is only a convenient length. The dashed line marks the cut after the fifth, and the label gives the fall in score across it as a share of the range from best to worst.

The four orders differ in ways that follow the physics of each series.

In the household, the lag of seven days is first, the sine and cosine of the hour are second and third, and the lags of two and three days follow. The weekday encodings rank tenth and eleventh, so the household repeats by the week through its own past and not through a weekday variable. Noise is last of twelve under every measure except the forest importance, which puts it eighth.

For EV charging the order starts with the lags of seven and two days, then the sine of the hour, the cosine of the hour and the lag of three days. The two weekday encodings and the noise are the last three.

The irradiance leads the PV output under all six measures. The lags of two and three days come next, then the panel temperature and the lag of seven days. Noise ranks twelfth of fourteen, above both weekday encodings, which suits an array whose output does not depend on the day of the week.

In the net load the lags of two, seven and three days are followed by the solar radiation. The air temperature is only ninth, behind two means of the past and two calendar variables, and noise is last of fourteen.

Across the four series noise sits last or within the lowest three. The forest importance misplaces it most often, ranking it above real inputs in the household, the PV output and the net load, and the fusion corrects that, which is the practical case for combining measures. The cut at five is not equally firm everywhere. The score falls by 12.7% of the range after the fifth input for the EV charging, a real break, but by only 2.2%, 3.5% and 4.8% for the household, the PV output and the net load, where the sixth input is almost as relevant as the fifth. Inputs that score near the noise column, as the weekday encodings do, can be dropped without loss. Relevance alone does not remove redundancy, however: the sine and cosine of the hour sit side by side in two of the four shortlists, although a model needs the pair only to place the hour on a circle.

Equal and Diversity Weights

Figure 8 sets the default order of twiga, the equal-weight Borda count, against the diversity-weighted one. The two orders select the same five inputs in all four series, and their rank correlation lies between 0.99 and 1.00. On this evidence the weighting changes little, and equal weights are enough.

    group = np.where(scores.index == "noise", "Noise", np.where(weighted <= 5, "Shortlist", "Other"))

Stability across Training Windows

A ranking helps little if it changes when a few more weeks of data arrive. Figure 9 repeats the whole analysis on the first 50%, 70% and 90% of each series, finding the lookback and the lags again each time. The best input is the same in all three windows for every series, and the top five are identical. The windows are nested, though, so they share data, and the check shows stability as data accumulate and not independence across periods. A later, disjoint period would be a stronger test, and a longer record would allow one. Noise is last in the household and the charging at every window, within the two lowest for the net load, and within the three lowest for the PV output, where two weekday encodings fall below it at 70% and 90%.

Limits of the Method

Relevance is not usefulness. Each measure scores one input at a time, so two inputs that carry the same information both rank high, and a shortlist can hold redundant inputs. The ranking is a shortlist for a forecaster to test and not a final choice. No forecaster is fitted here, so nothing shows that the shortlist forecasts better than all the candidates, and a comparison on held-out periods is the obvious next step, whose answer may differ by series. The weather inputs are treated as available over the forecast period, and with a real weather forecast their relevance would be lower.

The pool and the cut are fixed. The lags are calendar multiples of the detected period, so others, such as half-day multiples, are not in the pool, and the length of five is a convention. The selection reads the training window only, as the code here does. The function load_dataset of twiga applies the same functions to a whole file, which suits choosing a configuration for a dataset, whereas a backtest has to call them on the training window or the ranking sees the period that it is later tested on. Finally, the sample is small, since the findings describe one household, one site and one city and say nothing about how typical they are.

Recipe for Application

Every step uses the training window only.

  1. Hold out the period to be forecast, and keep the first part of the series in time.
  2. Find the periods of the series from its autocorrelation. The shortest sets the lookback window, and the longer ones become lag candidates, as get_best_autoregessive_features returns them.
  3. List the candidates by kind: the lags and rolling means, the sine and cosine of each calendar cycle, and the inputs known in advance. Add a column of noise.
  4. Rank each kind, then everything together. Keep the inputs that rank above the noise column and above a visible gap in the scores.
  5. Pass the shortlist to a forecaster, and test it against the full set of candidates on held-out periods.

Summary of the Method

For all four series the autocorrelation gives a window of one day and lags of two, three and seven days, which the daily cycle explains. The ranking then separates them. The lag of seven days is the best input for the household and the EV charging, the lag of two days for the net load, and the irradiance for the PV output. The hour is the only calendar variable to reach a shortlist, and the weekday encodings are among the lowest everywhere. Noise ranks last or within the lowest three in every series, although the forest importance puts it above real inputs in three, more often than any other measure. The top five are the same under equal and diversity weights and across the first 50%, 70% and 90% of each series, though those windows are nested. Ranking each subgroup first and applying a fixed quota selects the same inputs as the combined ranking for the household and the EV charging, and weaker calendar inputs for the PV output and the net load.

The ranking is a shortlist to test, and its length is better read from the gaps between scores than fixed in advance. The notebook and the two small data files are in the repository of this site. The EV series is downloaded when the notebook runs, and the code needs twiga[ml]==1.1.8 and lets-plot.

In Parts 1 and 2, we saw that while 80% of organisations run AI pilots, only 5% actually get measurable value. Those posts argued that this gap is mostly about strategy; many AI projects fail because they lack a clear focus, a guiding policy, or targeted actions. That explanation is still true, but it is not the full picture.

Some organisations have followed the advice from Parts 1 and 2. They have a clear focus, a solid strategy, and well-planned pilots. Yet, they still struggle to turn these efforts into real business value. Having a strategy and roadmap is important, but it is not enough. What is missing is a strong business model.

Osterwalder and Pigneur [1] say a business model is how an organisation creates, delivers, and captures value. Strategy is about direction and navigation. The business model explains how value is created, who benefits, how it is delivered, and how the organisation keeps enough value to keep going. In most tech shifts, the difference between strategy and business model is clear. With AI, though, all three parts change at once, often in ways old business models cannot handle. Without a framework for this, even a good AI strategy might not lead to revenue, a lasting advantage, or a clear reason for the investment.

This post tackles that problem. The AI Business Model Innovation Framework helps turn strategy into a business model that really captures AI value. It does not replace the roadmap from Part 2, but works underneath it, filling in the gaps that a roadmap alone cannot cover.

Why AI Breaks Existing Business Models

Before we look at the framework, let’s clarify what makes AI disruptive to business models, not just to strategy.

The three main AI features from Part 1 are clearly evident in business models. First, organisations often find out what AI can do before they know which customer problem it solves. This leads to products that talk about themselves instead of solving real problems. Second, revenue models based on today’s AI capabilities can quickly become outdated before the product can grow. Third, AI often creates value in ways that do not match up with when revenue is earned. Traditional business models, which link product delivery directly to payment, do not fit well with these AI realities.

Amazon Alexa is a good example of this problem. Technically, Alexa was impressive: top-notch voice recognition, strong platform integration, and devices in millions of homes. The AI strategy made sense, and the platform worked well. But the business model did not succeed. Most users only used Alexa for free features like timers, weather, and music. The revenue Amazon hoped for from shopping, subscriptions, and paid services never reached the needed scale. By 2022, the division was losing about ten billion dollars a year [2]. In 2023, Amazon restructured the team, cutting hundreds of jobs and quietly admitting the business model was not working.

The key question was never really answered before Alexa launched: what real problem would voice AI solve for a customer who would pay for it? This is not just a strategy issue; it is a business model issue. Organisations that mix up the two often end up with results like Alexa.

The AI Business Model Innovation Framework

The AI Business Model Innovation Framework has four parts: Data Foundation Establishment, Value-Centric Data Exploitation, Strategic AI Co-Innovation, and AI Value Realisation. The first three occur in order, while the fourth, AI Value Realisation, should be present throughout the process, not just at the end. This matters because many organisations treat value realisation as something to add after launch, but with AI, that approach fails. Value realisation needs to be built in from the beginning, right alongside the data foundation.

Figure 1 shows how the four elements connect. The rest of this section explains each one in detail.

Element 1: Data Foundation Establishment

The data foundation is the starting point for everything else. In terms of planning, it aligns with Step 2 in Part 2: honestly assessing the organisation’s data maturity, infrastructure, and governance.

From a business model perspective, the data foundation is more than just a technical need. In Helmer’s [3] framework, proprietary data is a Cornered Resource, something competitors cannot easily get. This is the stage when that resource is created or lost. If organisations treat data as something to fix later, they not only build up technical debt—they also lose a long-term advantage. Managing data well, connecting it across systems, and aligning it with business goals does more than prepare for AI. It creates a position that is hard for others to copy.

At this stage, the main tasks are updating data strategy and governance, finding the right data sources, building data pipelines, and running regular quality checks. [4] points out that overestimating data maturity is the top reason AI pilots fail. Many organisations think their data is better than it is, and only realise the problem after spending money and setting deadlines. Being honest here prevents that. Investing in the data foundation is not just a cost; it is the key asset for the whole framework.

Element 2: Value-Centric Data Exploitation

Once the data foundation is in place, the next step is to derive useful insights from the data and connect them to business goals. This is called value-centric data exploitation. It is not just about running technical queries—it means every analysis is tied to a clear business goal, not just exploring data for its own sake.

[5] calls this the point at which data shifts from being just an asset to a tool. This matters because data that does not answer a business question is just sitting there. Insights from value-centric exploitation serve as the basis for building AI models and creating new products or services.

The main activities here align with the guiding policy in Part 2. At this stage, developing or updating your AI strategy means ensuring your analysis aligns with the main challenge identified earlier. Improving AI governance, transforming data, extracting knowledge, and testing new ideas all help turn strategy into a business model.

Note

For example, a logistics company facing unpredictable last-mile deliveries does not analyse all its data. Instead, it focuses on route, weather, and demand data to support dynamic scheduling. Every insight is checked by asking: does this help solve the main problem? This focus is what makes value-centric exploitation different from just exploring data with a budget.

The result of this step is not just a tidy dataset. It is a set of proven insights that support a value proposition, along with a prototype to see whether customers would actually pay for it.

Element 3: Strategic AI Co-Innovation

The third element is where insights turn into products and the business model gets redesigned. This step is not just about improving current operations; it is about creating AI-powered offerings that can change the way business is done.

It is important to understand the difference between the two ways of using AI. Task augmentation means using AI to improve current processes, such as speeding up paperwork or improving forecasts. Autonomous systems use AI to create brand new products or services. Both are valid, but each leads to very different business models, revenue streams, costs, and competition.

Klarna’s AI assistant [6] shows this difference well. Instead of just speeding up its customer service team, Klarna replaced about 700 agents with an AI system that handled two-thirds of all chats in its first month. This was not just improving a task—it was a whole new way of working, with a new cost structure and a new way to capture value. The business model changed, and this shift came from co-innovating with partners and the AI itself, not just following a roadmap.

Key activities here include developing an AI strategy aligned with co-innovation goals, identifying opportunities for both task improvement and new autonomous systems, forming partnerships, and testing AI-powered products in small-scale settings before a full launch. Working with external partners is especially important now, since most organisations lack the full range of skills needed for real AI co-innovation. Those willing to co-design with others rather than work alone are the ones who truly change their business models.

At this stage, actions should be driven by clear questions, just like in Part 2. Every experiment should test a specific idea about a real problem. Without this focus, co-innovation can lead to lots of impressive technology but no clear value for customers.

Element 4: AI Value Realisation

AI Value Realisation is not just the last step. It is a practice that should be present from the start—when building the data foundation, during data use and co-innovation, and all the way through to product launch. Treating it as something to do at the end leads to problems, like IBM Watson Health measuring agreement rates instead of real clinical results, or Amazon Alexa counting device activations instead of actual value per user.

The element has three interdependent components: Value Architecture, Monetisation, and Valuation.

Value Architecture makes sure AI projects are built around a clear value proposition for a specific group of customers. It asks the tough questions early: who is this for, what problem does it solve, how is it different from competitors, and how do we explain that difference? Without this, the AI project might work technically, but no one will want to buy it.

Monetisation turns the value architecture into a means of making money. This should be done before starting development, not after. Setting up revenue streams, cost structures, and linking AI projects to long-term strategy is much easier to plan from the start than to add later. Palantir is a good example; they set up contracts based on outcomes, not just software access. Customers pay for solutions, not licenses. This approach made Palantir define exactly what problems they were solving before setting a price, so the business model and problem-solving went hand in hand.

Valuation is the final piece. In AI, common KPIs like model accuracy or deployment numbers measure technology, not business results. As [7] points out, real AI value comes from better workflows and decisions at scale, not just from launching a model. The important KPIs are those that show if the main problem has been solved—like faster decisions, fewer errors, or customer issues fixed. These are harder to track, but they are the only ones that show if the business model works.

Table 1 summarises the three components and the question each one forces.

The Capabilities That Make It Work

The four elements need a base of technology, organisation, and leadership skills to work. These are not extra steps; they are the conditions needed for the framework to succeed.

Technological capabilities include data infrastructure, AI platforms, cloud computing, and analytics. Organisational capabilities mean having a data-driven culture, skilled AI staff, and good governance. Together, these create an environment where AI can deliver real value, not just technical results.

Leadership skills are often overlooked but are the most important. As [7] explains, AI-native organisations do more than just use AI tools; they change how decisions are made, shifting authority from people to algorithms in planned ways. This is a leadership choice, not just a tech upgrade. The organisations that get the most value from AI are those where leaders understand this shift and make it happen on purpose, not by accident.

When these capabilities are missing, the problem is not with technology—it is with structure. AI teams and business teams work separately, each focused on their own goals, and neither sees the full business model. The framework requires both groups to work together from the start, agreeing on the main challenge and designing value realisation before building the data foundation or product roadmap.

How to Spot a Bad AI Business Model

The four-part framework also works as a diagnostic tool. When used on any AI project, it reveals problems that most organisations only notice after they have already invested.

Sometimes, the value proposition focuses on the technology instead of the customer. The organisation can explain what its AI does, but not what problem it solves for a specific buyer. For example, IBM Watson Health’s marketing talked about what Watson could do with data, but never clearly said which clinical outcome it improved, for which patients, or in what setting. A value proposition based on features, not real problems, does not help customers decide to buy.

Monetisation is retrofitted. The revenue model was designed after the product was built, which means it captures activity rather than value. Platform subscriptions, per-seat licensing, and usage fees charge for access to a capability rather than for problem resolution. Outcome-linked revenue models require a precise definition of the outcome before the contract can be written. That discipline forces the diagnostic precision that activity-based models allow organisations to avoid. Organisations that retrofit monetisation consistently end up with a revenue model that the customer’s buying process was never designed to accommodate.

Sometimes, valuation focuses on the wrong things. KPIs like model accuracy, response times, or deployment numbers measure technology, not whether the main problem is solved. An organisation can show great tech results but still not fix the business issue that justified the investment. This is not just a measurement problem—it is a design problem. The valuation system was set up before the value architecture was clear, so it measured what was easy, not what mattered.

Sometimes, organisations build up AI talent, data platforms, and governance, but leaders keep making decisions the same way as before. The technology is there, but the real organisational change needed to create value is missing. This is called capabilities theatre—it looks like the organisation is ready for AI, but the decision-making has not changed.

These four failure modes are connected. If an organisation does not have a clear value proposition, it will add monetisation later because there is nothing specific to price. When monetisation is added late, it usually relies on activity metrics, since outcomes were never defined. Activity metrics do not show if decision-making has changed, so the capability gap stays hidden—until a competitor with the right model exposes the problem.

Conclusion: Strategy, Roadmap, Business Model

Parts 1 and 2 showed that the gap between 80% of organisations running AI pilots and the 5% getting real value is mostly about strategy. That is still true, but there is another layer. If organisations fix their strategy but do not update their business model, they are just making the same mistake in a different direction.

The AI Business Model Innovation Framework is the missing piece under the roadmap. The data foundation is where you build or lose your unique resource. Value-centric exploitation turns data into the base for AI innovation, not just storage. Strategic co-innovation is when you truly redesign the business model. AI Value Realisation, present throughout, makes sure value architecture, monetisation, and valuation are planned together, not added later.

Together, these three posts form a complete story. The kernel and roadmap show you where to go and how to get there. The business model innovation framework explains how value is created, who benefits, what it costs, and how to measure success. You need both parts; they are what set the 5% apart from the 80%.

The real question is not if you need a business model, but whether you design it before you invest or after you have already spent the money.
